candidate.answerReason: The 12 dollars above a one-dollar-per-pair baseline consist of two-dollar and three-dollar increases. Positivity and parity force two four-dollar pairs and three three-dollar pairs, leaving seven one-dollar pairs. This agrees with choice D.

methods.label: Track the extra cost
methods.explanation:
If all \(12\) pairs had cost \(\$1\) each, the total would have been \(\$12\). Ralph actually spent \(\$24\), so the more expensive pairs account for \(\$12\) in extra cost. Each \(\$3\) pair adds \(\$2\), and each \(\$4\) pair adds \(\$3\).

The number of \(\$4\) pairs must be even. All the \(\$2\) increases total an even number, and an odd number of \(\$3\) increases would make the overall extra cost odd instead of \(12\).

There must be at least one \(\$4\) pair, but there cannot be four or more: four of their \(\$3\) increases would use the entire \(\$12\), leaving nothing for the required \(\$3\) pair. The only positive even count below four is \(2\).

Those two pairs use \(2\cdot3=6\) dollars of extra cost. The remaining \(12-6=6\) dollars pay for \(6\div2=3\) of the \(\$3\) pairs. Therefore the number of \(\$1\) pairs is
\[
12-2-3=\boxed{7}.
\]
Indeed, \(7+3\cdot3+2\cdot4=24\), with at least one pair of every type. The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: The reasoning uses a simple price baseline and odd/even totals. No formal congruences or systems of equations are needed.

methods.label: Bound the number of cheapest pairs
methods.explanation:
Compare the possible total costs when Ralph buys too few or too many \(\$1\) pairs.

If he buys at most \(6\) of the \(\$1\) pairs, the cheapest purchase satisfying all the conditions has six \(\$1\) pairs, five \(\$3\) pairs, and one \(\$4\) pair. Its cost is
\[
6+5\cdot3+4=25.
\]
Using fewer \(\$1\) pairs or more \(\$4\) pairs only increases this cost. Thus at most six cheap pairs would cost more than \(\$24\).

If he buys at least \(8\) of the \(\$1\) pairs, the most expensive allowed purchase has eight \(\$1\) pairs, one \(\$3\) pair, and three \(\$4\) pairs. Its cost is
\[
8+3+3\cdot4=23.
\]
Using more \(\$1\) pairs leaves fewer expensive pairs, and replacing a \(\$4\) pair by a \(\$3\) pair also lowers the cost. Thus at least eight cheap pairs would cost less than \(\$24\).

The only remaining integer count is \(7\). It works: seven \(\$1\) pairs, three \(\$3\) pairs, and two \(\$4\) pairs make \(12\) pairs costing \(7+9+8=24\) dollars. Therefore the answer is \(\boxed{7}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
